blocks.x: 2026’s Most Savage Horror Sleeper Hit Is Officially Unleashed on Streaming

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

Horror fans have been truly blessed in 2026. YouTuber Mark Edward Fischbach (aka Markiplier) surprised everyone with an early-year surprise in Iron Lung; Adam Scott followed up on the latest season of Severance with Hokum; Nia DaCosta directed one of the year's best horrors with 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple; Kane Parsons blew minds with his directorial debut Backrooms; Curry Barker's breakout masterpiece Obsession is a record-breaking phenomenon, and much more.

One of the best early horror movies that has arguably gone under the radar is Send Help, a Rachel McAdams-led survival horror that marked the return of director Sam Raimi to the genre after many years away. Many months later, the franchise that first put Raimi on the map also returned in fiery fashion in the form of Infested director Sébastien Vaniček's Evil Dead Burn. The movie stars Souheila Yacoub as Alice, a grieving widow who visits her late husband’s family following the funeral, only for everything to go very wrong very quickly.

The sixth movie in the Evil Dead franchise, and, of course, featuring a blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo from Bruce Campbell, Evil Dead Burn was an undeniable hit at the box office, scoring a global haul of $72 million against a reported budget of $20 million. The film debuted in fourth on the domestic charts before bowing out over six weeks later. Since then, the film has finally made its way to streaming and is proving a hit once again. At the time of writing, Evil Dead Burn is one of the most-watched movies on HBO Max in the U.S.

A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.
You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
